title: Review: Kinetic theory of gases; Gas laws and ideal gas equation; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium; Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics 2 (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: T01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; T03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; T03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: T01-1#N.5, T03-1#N.7b, T05-1#N.6, T06-1#N.4b, T01-1#N.11, T03-1#N.11, T05-1#N.12, T06-1#N.14, T01-1#N.2, T03-1#N.4, T05-1#N.9c, T03-1#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Heat
items.clue: Energy in transit because of a temperature difference; a body does not contain it.

items.label: Conduction
items.clue: Transfer passed from particle to particle through a material that itself stays put.

items.label: Internal energy
items.clue: Total of the random kinetic and potential contributions of all the particles in a body.

items.label: Radiation
items.clue: Transfer by electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared at everyday temperatures; crosses a vacuum.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: A brick wall has area 12 m² and thickness 0.20 m; its thermal conductivity is 0.60 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Its inner face is at 18 °C and its outer face at 3 °C. What is the rate of energy transfer through the wall by conduction?

Predict first. Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot pressure against temperature in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to zero pressure. What do they find?

options.text: All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, 0 °C.
All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, about −273 °C.
The steepest line reaches zero pressure at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches zero pressure at a temperature set by its kind of gas.

questions.stem: A rigid, sealed container holds an ideal gas. The absolute temperature of the gas is doubled. Using the kinetic model, in which the pressure comes from atoms colliding with the walls, by what factor is the pressure of the gas multiplied?
A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.

questions.stem: Two slabs, P and Q, have the same area and the same thickness, and the same temperature difference is held across each. P is copper (k = 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) and Q is glass (k = 0.80 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Which statement about the rates of energy transfer by conduction is correct?

options.text: The rates are equal, because the temperature difference across each slab is the same.
The rate through Q is greater, because glass stores more thermal energy than copper does.
The rate through P is greater only while P is colder than Q; it then falls to the same value.
The rate through P is about 500 times the rate through Q.

questions.explanation: Same A, same ΔT, same thickness, so rate ∝ k. 400 ÷ 0.80 = 500.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds an ideal gas at 7 °C. The gas is heated to 287 °C. How does its new pressure compare with its starting pressure?

options.text: It is the same, because the container is rigid, so the volume cannot change.
It is 41 times as large, because the temperature has risen from 7 °C to 287 °C.
It is twice as large, because the absolute temperature doubles, from 280 K to 560 K.
It is 1.4 times as large, because the molecules move √2 times as fast.

questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure ÷ absolute temperature is constant. 560 K/280 K = 2.

questions.stem: A container holds a mixture of hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂) at one temperature. An oxygen molecule has 16 times the mass of a hydrogen molecule. What is (rms speed of the hydrogen molecules)/(rms speed of the oxygen molecules)?

options.text: 1, because the two gases are at the same temperature.
16, because the hydrogen molecules have 1/16 of the mass.
1/4, because the heavier molecules hit harder and so move faster.
4, because equal mean kinetic energies mean speed ∝ 1/√m.

questions.explanation: ½m(rms speed)², the mean kinetic energy, depends only on T, so it is the same for both, so rms speed ∝ 1/√m = √16 = 4.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the net thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: One end of a glass rod is held in a flame. How does the molecular model explain conduction of energy along the rod?

options.text: Hot particles travel along the rod from the hot end to the cold end, carrying their energy with them.
Faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their slower neighbours, and so on along the rod.
Heat flows along the rod like a fluid, filling the spaces between the particles as it goes.
Particles at the hot end expand and push against their neighbours, passing the heat along.

questions.stem: A rigid steel tank contains an ideal gas at 27°C and a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. A valve is opened until half of the gas has escaped, and then the gas remaining in the tank is heated to 327°C. What is the pressure of the gas now?
In some refrigerators the cooling unit is at the top of the cabinet, not the bottom. Why does this cool the whole cabinet well?

options.text: Cold spreads out evenly from the cooling unit in every direction, so where it sits makes no difference.
Air cooled at the top is denser and sinks; warmer air rises to the unit, so a current circulates.
Heat rises to the top of the cabinet, where the unit can remove it before it spreads out.
The unit cools mostly by radiation, which travels downwards through the air to the food.

questions.explanation: Cooled air contracts, so it is denser than the air below and sinks. Warmer, less dense air is pushed up to the unit: a convection current through the whole cabinet.
